source.text: Καὶ συνάγονται πρὸς αὐτὸν οἱ Φαρισαῖοι καί τινες τῶν γραμματέων ἐλθόντες ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων καὶ ἰδόντες τινὰς τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ ὅτι κοιναῖς χερσίν, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ἀνίπτοις, ἐσθίουσιν τοὺς ἄρτους οἱ γὰρ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ πάντες οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἐὰν μὴ πυγμῇ νίψωνται τὰς χεῖρας οὐκ ἐσθίουσιν, κρατοῦντες τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ ἀπ’ ἀγορᾶς ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται οὐκ ἐσθίουσιν, καὶ ἄλλα πολλά ἐστιν ἃ παρέλαβον κρατεῖν, βαπτισμοὺς ποτηρίων καὶ ξεστῶν καὶ χαλκίων καὶ κλινῶν καὶ ἐπερωτῶσιν αὐτὸν οἱ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς· Διὰ τί οὐ περιπατοῦσιν οἱ μαθηταί σου κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, ἀλλὰ κοιναῖς χερσὶν ἐσθίουσιν τὸν ἄρτον;

records.literal_gloss: And are gathered together to him the Pharisees and some of the scribes having come from Jerusalem \v 2 and having seen some of the disciples of him that with defiled hands, that is, unwashed, they eat the loaves \v 3 (for the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless with [the] fist they wash the hands, not eat, holding the tradition of the elders, \v 4 and from [the] marketplace, unless they wash themselves, not eat, and other things many there are which they received to hold, washings of cups and pitchers and copper vessels and couches) \v 5 and question him the Pharisees and the scribes, Why not walk the disciples of you according to the tradition of the elders, but with defiled hands eat the bread?

en.L: And the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gather to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \v 2 and [they] had seen that some of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples eat [their] bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed \v 3 (for the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash [their] hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders, \v 4 and [coming] from the marketplace they do not eat unless they wash themselves, and there are many other things which they have received to hold to, washings of cups and pitchers and bronze vessels and couches), \v 5 and the Pharisees and the scribes question {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Why do {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat [their] bread with defiled hands?"
en.B: The Pharisees gathered around Jesus, together with some scribes who had come from Jerusalem. \v 2 They had noticed that some of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples were eating their food with unclean hands, that is, hands not washed. \v 3 (The Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, will not eat unless they give their hands a ritual washing, and so they keep the tradition of the elders. \v 4 When they come in from the marketplace they do not eat without first washing. They hold to many other customs that have been passed on to them as well, such as the washing of cups, pitchers, bronze pots and dining couches.) \v 5 So the Pharisees and the scribes put a question to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Why do {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} disciples not live by the tradition of the elders? Why do they eat with unclean hands?"
en.R: Some Pharisees and some teachers of God's law came from Jerusalem. They gathered around Jesus. \v 2 They saw that some of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers were eating food without first washing their hands in the special religious way. \v 3 The Pharisees, like all Jewish people, would not eat unless they had washed their hands in this special way. In this way they kept the rules handed down by their teachers from long ago. \v 4 When they came home from the market, they would not eat until they had washed. They also kept many other rules like these. They washed cups, pitchers, and metal pots in a special way, and even the couches they lay on to eat. \v 5 So the Pharisees and the teachers of God's law asked Jesus, "Why do {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} followers not obey the rules our teachers handed down? They eat their food with hands that have not been made clean!"

decisions.choice: are gathered, question: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid. The sense is past: they gathered, and they asked.

decisions.choice: defiled hands: hands that had not been washed by the ritual, so counted unclean, not dirty
decisions.reason: The word means common, ordinary, and so not set apart as clean. The washing was a religious rite, not a matter of hygiene. Mark explains this to readers who did not know Jewish custom.

decisions.choice: Mark stops the story to explain Jewish washing customs
decisions.reason: Verses 3-4 are Mark's note to his readers, many of whom were not Jews. The sentence that began in verse 1 is broken off and picked up again in verse 5.

decisions.choice: with the fist: a particular ritual way of washing, whose exact form is uncertain
alternatives: with a cupped handful of water
decisions.reason: The word means a fist. It may describe pouring water over the hands held in a fist, rubbing one fist in the other palm, or washing up to the wrist. All agree it names a set way of washing.

decisions.choice: with the fist, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "often" and a few leave the word out, perhaps because scribes found "with the fist" hard to understand. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the tradition of the elders: rules taught by earlier teachers and passed on by word of mouth
decisions.reason: The elders here are teachers of past generations. Their rulings, added to the law of Moses, were held by the Pharisees to be binding. The washing of hands before ordinary meals is not commanded in the law of Moses.

decisions.choice: from the marketplace: when they come back from the market, they wash before eating
alternatives: they do not eat food from the market unless they wash it
decisions.reason: The words can be read either way. Most likely contact with many people at the market was thought to make a person unclean.

decisions.choice: wash themselves, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts read "sprinkle themselves". The SBLGNT reads the verb that means to wash or dip, the word from which baptize comes. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: and couches: in the SBLGNT text
decisions.reason: Several early manuscripts do not have "and couches", perhaps because scribes thought it strange to wash couches. The couches were those people reclined on to eat. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: give their hands a ritual washing
alternatives: wash their hands with the fist
decisions.reason: The exact sense of "with the fist" is unknown. Balanced gives what is certain: a set religious washing.

decisions.choice: the rules handed down by their teachers from long ago; the couches they lay on to eat
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the elders were and what couches were washed.

source.text: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Καλῶς ἐπροφήτευσεν Ἠσαΐας περὶ ὑμῶν τῶν ὑποκριτῶν, ὡς γέγραπται ὅτι Οὗτος ὁ λαὸς τοῖς χείλεσίν με τιμᾷ, ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ·

records.literal_gloss: And he said to them, Well prophesied Isaiah about you the hypocrites, as it has been written, This people with the lips me honors, but the heart of them far is away from me;

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy about you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with [their] lips, but their heart is far away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}};
en.B: He answered them, "How well Isaiah prophesied about you hypocrites! As it stands written: 'This people gives {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} honor with their lips, while their heart stays far away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.R: Jesus answered them, "You are hypocrites. You pretend to be good, but you are not. Isaiah was right about you when he spoke God's message long ago. He wrote down what God said: 'These people say that they honor {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, but it is only words from their lips. Their hearts are far away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 29:13, in the wording of the ancient Greek translation
decisions.reason: Jesus quotes God's complaint through Isaiah against a people whose worship was only outward. The wording follows the Greek translation of Isaiah closely.

decisions.choice: hypocrites: people who play a part, whose outward show does not match the heart
decisions.reason: The word was used for an actor on a stage. The quotation shows the meaning: honor with the lips while the heart is far away. This is the only time Mark uses it.

decisions.choice: prophesied well: spoke God's word truly and to the point
decisions.reason: To prophesy is to speak for God. Isaiah's words fit the people of his own day, and Jesus says they fit these men too.

decisions.choice: lips and heart: God looks for worship that comes from within
decisions.reason: The heart is the center of thought and will. This prepares for 7:21, where evil comes from the heart.

decisions.choice: You pretend to be good, but you are not
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word hypocrite.

decisions.choice: say that they honor me, but it is only words from their lips
decisions.reason: Readable says what honoring with the lips means.

source.text: μάτην δὲ σέβονταί με, διδάσκοντες διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων·

records.literal_gloss: in vain and they worship me, teaching [as] teachings commands of men.

en.L: and in vain they worship {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, teaching as doctrines the commands of {{gender:people|men}}.'
en.B: Their worship of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is worthless, for they pass off human commands as doctrine.'
en.R: Their worship of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is useless. They teach rules that people made up as if they were God's teaching.'

decisions.choice: the end of Isaiah 29:13 in the Greek translation
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of Isaiah says that their fear of God is a command of men learned by rote. The Greek translation, which Mark follows, says that their worship is in vain because they teach human commands. The sense is close.

decisions.choice: in vain: to no purpose, empty
decisions.reason: Their worship achieves nothing with God.

decisions.choice: teaching human commands as doctrines: passing off their own rules as God's teaching
decisions.reason: The verb takes two objects: what they teach, human commands, and what they present them as, doctrines.

decisions.choice: people (men as the alternative)
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general, as against God.

source.text: ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων.

records.literal_gloss: Having left the commandment of the God you hold the tradition of the men.

en.L: Leaving the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of {{gender:people|men}}."
en.B: You abandon what God has commanded and hold fast to a tradition that is merely human."
en.R: You put God's command to one side, and you hold on to rules that came from people."

decisions.choice: leaving: abandoning, letting go
decisions.reason: The verb can mean forgive, but here it means to leave behind or neglect.

decisions.choice: the commandment of God: God's law as a whole
decisions.reason: The singular sums up what God has commanded. Verse 10 gives an example.

decisions.choice: God's command against human tradition: the contrast that runs through 7:8-13
decisions.reason: Jesus does not reject every custom. He rejects tradition that is held in place of God's command.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT ends the verse at "the tradition of men"
alternatives: add: the washing of pitchers and cups, and many other such things you do
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add these words, which repeat 7:4 and 7:13. They are not in the earliest manuscripts. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: a tradition that is merely human
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the contrast with God's command.

source.text: Καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Καλῶς ἀθετεῖτε τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἵνα τὴν παράδοσιν ὑμῶν τηρήσητε·

records.literal_gloss: And he was saying to them, Well you set aside the commandment of the God so that the tradition of you you might keep.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to them, "Well do you set aside the commandment of God, so that you may keep your tradition.
en.B: He went on, "You are very skillful at setting God's command aside so that you can keep your own tradition!
en.R: Jesus went on, "You are very clever! You find ways to ignore what God commands so that you can keep your own rules.

decisions.choice: well: said with irony, how cleverly
decisions.reason: The same word as in 7:6, now turned against them: they are skilled at the wrong thing.

decisions.choice: set aside: reject, treat as void
decisions.reason: The verb is used for refusing or cancelling something that has force.

decisions.choice: keep, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "establish" your tradition. The two words differ by little in Greek. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: very skillful (B); very clever (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the irony of "well" plain.

source.text: Μωϋσῆς γὰρ εἶπεν· Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα σου, καί· Ὁ κακολογῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα θανάτῳ τελευτάτω·

records.literal_gloss: Moses for said, Honor the father of you and the mother of you, and, The [one] speaking evil of father or mother by death let him end.

en.L: For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must surely die.'
en.B: For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and also, 'Whoever reviles father or mother is to die for it.'
en.R: Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother.' He also said, 'Anyone who says evil things against their father or mother is to be put to death.'

decisions.choice: honor your father and your mother: the fifth commandment, Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16
decisions.reason: Jesus calls the commandment the word of Moses here and the word of God in 7:13.

decisions.choice: whoever speaks evil of father or mother: Exodus 21:17; Leviticus 20:9
decisions.reason: The law treated cursing a parent as a crime deserving death.

decisions.choice: honor: respect, and also support and care for parents in old age
decisions.reason: Honoring parents included providing for them. This is the point of the example in 7:11-12.

decisions.choice: end by death: surely die, be put to death
decisions.reason: The words copy a Hebrew way of speaking that stresses certainty. The law means the death penalty.

decisions.choice: reviles
decisions.reason: The verb means to speak evil of someone, to abuse with words.

source.text: ὑμεῖς δὲ λέγετε· Ἐὰν εἴπῃ ἄνθρωπος τῷ πατρὶ ἢ τῇ μητρί· Κορβᾶν, ὅ ἐστιν Δῶρον, ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, οὐκέτι ἀφίετε αὐτὸν οὐδὲν ποιῆσαι τῷ πατρὶ ἢ τῇ μητρί, ἀκυροῦντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ παραδόσει ὑμῶν ᾗ παρεδώκατε· καὶ παρόμοια τοιαῦτα πολλὰ ποιεῖτε.

records.literal_gloss: You but say, If says a man to the father or the mother, Corban, which is, Gift, whatever from me you might be benefited, \v 12 no longer you allow him anything to do for the father or the mother, \v 13 making void the word of the God by the tradition of you which you handed down; and similar such things many you do.

en.L: But you say, 'If a person says to father or mother, "Whatever you might have gained from me [is] Corban," which is, a gift [to God],' \v 12 you no longer let that person do anything for father or mother, \v 13 making void the word of God by your tradition which you have handed down; and you do many similar things such as these."
en.B: But you teach that if someone tells father or mother, 'Whatever support you could have had from me is Corban' (which means an offering to God), \v 12 then you no longer let that person do anything for their father or mother. \v 13 You make God's word empty for the sake of the tradition you hand down, and you do plenty of other things of the same kind."
en.R: But you teach something else. You say that a person can tell their father or mother, 'I cannot help you, because what I would have given you is Corban.' Corban means a gift set apart for God. \v 12 After that, you will not let them do anything to help their father or mother. \v 13 So by keeping the rules you pass down, you make God's word count for nothing. And you do many other things like that."

decisions.choice: Corban: a word for an offering dedicated to God, kept and translated by Mark
decisions.reason: The word is used in the law of Moses for an offering brought to God (Leviticus 2:1). A man could declare his goods Corban, set apart for God, and so put them beyond his parents' reach, while he may still have kept the use of them.

decisions.choice: the sentence is left unfinished: Jesus states their rule, then says what follows from it
decisions.reason: The teachers' rule is "if anyone says Corban, the vow stands". Jesus breaks off and states the result: you no longer allow him to help his parents.

decisions.choice: making void: cancelling, taking away the force of
decisions.reason: The word was used for annulling a law or a contract.

decisions.choice: the word of God: the commandment Moses gave (7:10)
decisions.reason: What Moses said in 7:10 Jesus calls the word of God, set against the tradition handed down by people.

decisions.choice: Corban, kept as Mark keeps it
decisions.reason: Mark keeps the Hebrew word and explains it, so every level does the same.

decisions.choice: I cannot help you, because
decisions.reason: Readable says what the vow meant for the parents.

source.text: Καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος πάλιν τὸν ὄχλον ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Ἀκούσατέ μου πάντες καὶ σύνετε.

records.literal_gloss: And having called to [him] again the crowd he was saying to them, Hear me all and understand.

en.L: And calling the crowd to [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] again, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to them, "Hear {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, all [of you], and understand:
en.B: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} called the crowd to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} once more and said, "Hear {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, every one of you, and understand this:
en.R: Then Jesus called the crowd to come to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} again. He said, "Everyone, listen to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and try to understand.

decisions.choice: again: once more Jesus calls the crowd to hear
alternatives: the crowd had been there all along
decisions.reason: The crowd were last named in 6:55-56. Jesus now turns from the Pharisees to teach everyone.

decisions.choice: understand: grasp the meaning
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in 4:12 and 6:52. The disciples will show in 7:18 that they have not understood.

decisions.choice: try to understand
decisions.reason: Readable shows that this is a call to think carefully.

source.text: οὐδέν ἐστιν ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς αὐτὸν ὃ δύναται κοινῶσαι αὐτόν· ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκπορευόμενά ἐστιν τὰ κοινοῦντα τὸν ἄνθρωπον.

records.literal_gloss: Nothing there is from outside the man entering into him which is able to defile him; but the things out of the man going out are the things defiling the man.

en.L: There is nothing from outside the person that enters into {{gender:them|him}} which can defile {{gender:them|him}}; but the things coming out of the person are the things that defile the person."
en.B: Nothing outside a person can make that person unclean by going in. What comes out of a person is what makes a person unclean."
en.R: Nothing that goes into people from the outside can make them unclean before God. It is the things that come out of people that make them unclean."

decisions.choice: defile: make common, that is, ritually unclean
decisions.reason: The verb is formed from the word for the "defiled" hands of 7:2. Unclean means unfit to come before God in worship.

decisions.choice: the man: any human being
decisions.reason: The word means a person, man or woman.

decisions.choice: true uncleanness comes from within, not from food
alternatives: a teaching only about washing hands
decisions.reason: Jesus goes further than the question about hands. What enters the body cannot make a person unclean; what comes from the heart does (7:21-23). Mark draws out the meaning for food in 7:19.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT has no verse 16
alternatives: add verse 16: If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add verse 16, "If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear." It is missing from the earliest manuscripts and was most likely copied from 4:9 and 4:23, where Jesus says the same after a parable. The SBLGNT leaves it out, so the verse number 16 is skipped. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: them (him as the alternative) in Literal; a person, people in Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: The saying is about every person, so the wording is inclusive.

decisions.choice: unclean before God
decisions.reason: Readable says before whom a person is unclean.

source.text: Καὶ ὅτε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς οἶκον ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου, ἐπηρώτων αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν παραβολήν.

records.literal_gloss: And when he entered into a house from the crowd, were asking him the disciples of him the parable.

en.L: And when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} entered into a house away from the crowd, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples were asking {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [about] the parable.
en.B: When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had left the crowd and gone indoors, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} about this parable.
en.R: Jesus left the crowd and went into a house. Then {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} what this word picture meant.

decisions.choice: parable: a puzzling saying that needs to be explained
decisions.reason: The parable is the short saying of 7:15. The word can mean a riddle or dark saying as well as a story.

decisions.choice: into a house: away from the crowd, as in 4:10
decisions.reason: Mark does not name the house. As in 4:10-20, Jesus explains his sayings to the disciples in private.

decisions.choice: word picture
decisions.reason: Readable keeps its usual wording for a parable.

source.text: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀσύνετοί ἐστε;

records.literal_gloss: And he says to them, Thus also you without understanding are?

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to them, "Are you also so without understanding?
en.B: He said to them, "Are even you so slow to understand?
en.R: Jesus said to them, "Do even you not understand this?

decisions.choice: without understanding: unable to grasp the meaning
decisions.reason: The word answers 7:14, where Jesus called everyone to understand. The disciples are no quicker than the crowd (6:52; 8:17).

decisions.choice: a question that rebukes
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates the words as a question. Jesus is surprised that his own followers need an explanation.

source.text: οὐ νοεῖτε ὅτι πᾶν τὸ ἔξωθεν εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς τὸν ἄνθρωπον οὐ δύναται αὐτὸν κοινῶσαι, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσπορεύεται αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν καρδίαν ἀλλ’ εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν, καὶ εἰς τὸν ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκπορεύεται;

records.literal_gloss: Not you understand that everything from outside entering into the man not is able him to defile, \v 19 because not it enters of him into the heart but into the belly, and into the latrine goes out?

en.L: Do you not perceive that everything entering into the person from outside cannot defile {{gender:them|him}}, \v 19 because it does not enter into {{gender:their|his}} heart but into the belly, and goes out into the latrine?"
en.B: Do you not see that nothing that goes into a person from outside can make that person unclean? \v 19 It does not go into the heart but into the stomach, and from there it goes out into the latrine."
en.R: Do you not see? Nothing that goes into people from the outside can make them unclean. \v 19 It does not go into their hearts. It goes into their stomachs, and then it goes out of their bodies into the toilet."

decisions.choice: heart: the inner self, the center of thought and will
decisions.reason: Food goes into the stomach, not into the heart where a person's choices are made (7:21).

decisions.choice: latrine: the place where waste goes
decisions.reason: The word means a privy or toilet. Jesus speaks plainly: food passes through the body and out of it.

decisions.choice: do you not perceive: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: Jesus states what they ought to have seen for themselves.

decisions.choice: toilet
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word.

source.text: καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα.

records.literal_gloss: cleansing all the foods.

en.L: [In this {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was] making all foods clean.
en.B: By saying this, Jesus made all foods clean.
en.R: When Jesus said this, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was making all foods clean. People could eat any kind of food.

decisions.choice: making clean: Mark's comment on Jesus' words, with Jesus as the one who makes clean
alternatives: the digestive process cleans the food
decisions.reason: The word is a participle that is masculine and goes with the speaker of 7:18, "he says". It cannot go with the latrine or with the food that enters. So it is Mark's own note: by this teaching Jesus declared all foods clean. Older translations read it as part of Jesus' words, about the body purging food.

decisions.choice: making clean, a masculine form, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: a neuter form, linking the words to the process of digestion
decisions.reason: Some later manuscripts have a neuter form, which ties the words to what goes on in the body. The earliest manuscripts have the masculine form. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: all foods clean: the food laws no longer decide who is clean before God
alternatives: only food eaten with unwashed hands
decisions.reason: The food laws of Leviticus 11 separated clean from unclean animals. Mark sees in Jesus' words that this division is now ended. The same verb is used in Peter's vision, "what God has made clean" (Acts 10:15; compare Romans 14:14, 20).

decisions.choice: a sentence of its own, set apart from Jesus' words
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT closes Jesus' question at "goes out into the latrine" and sets these words apart as Mark's comment.

decisions.choice: [In this he was] (L); By saying this, Jesus (B); When Jesus said this (R)
alternatives: cleansing all foods, with no subject
decisions.reason: English needs a subject and must show that this is the writer's comment, not Jesus' words.

decisions.choice: People could eat any kind of food
decisions.reason: Readable says what making all foods clean meant in practice.

source.text: ἔλεγεν δὲ ὅτι Τὸ ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκεῖνο κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον·

records.literal_gloss: He was saying and that, That which out of the man going out, that defiles the man.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying, "What comes out of the person, that defiles the person.
en.B: He went on, "What comes out of a person is what makes a person unclean.
en.R: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "It is what comes out of people that makes them unclean.

decisions.choice: that defiles: the word "that" stresses what comes out
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats the second half of 7:15 and goes on to explain it.

decisions.choice: he was saying: Jesus continues speaking to the disciples
decisions.reason: The imperfect continues the private teaching in the house.

source.text: ἔσωθεν γὰρ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ διαλογισμοὶ οἱ κακοὶ ἐκπορεύονται, πορνεῖαι, κλοπαί, φόνοι, μοιχεῖαι, πλεονεξίαι, πονηρίαι, δόλος, ἀσέλγεια, ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός, βλασφημία, ὑπερηφανία, ἀφροσύνη·

records.literal_gloss: From within for out of the heart of the men the thoughts the evil go out, sexual immoralities, thefts, murders, \v 22 adulteries, covetings, wickednesses, deceit, sensuality, eye evil, slander, pride, foolishness;

en.L: For from within, out of the heart of {{gender:people|men}}, come the evil thoughts, sexual immoralities, thefts, murders, \v 22 adulteries, greedy desires, wickednesses, deceit, sensuality, an evil eye, slander, pride, foolishness;
en.B: Out of the human heart, from within, come evil designs, sexual sin, theft, murder, \v 22 adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, envy, slander, pride, and moral folly.
en.R: Evil things come from inside a person, from the heart. These include evil plans, sexual sin, stealing, and murder. \v 22 They also include adultery, greed, doing harm to others, lying and cheating, shameless living, jealousy, saying evil things about others, pride, and living like a fool.

decisions.choice: evil thoughts, then twelve evils: six acts in the plural, six traits in the singular
alternatives: evil thoughts as a heading for all that follow
decisions.reason: Evil thoughts come first, as the root. The plurals name deeds done again and again; the singulars name attitudes of the heart.

decisions.choice: sexual immorality: any sexual sin outside marriage
decisions.reason: The word is broad. Adultery, breaking one's own marriage, is named separately.

decisions.choice: an evil eye: envy, grudging meanness
alternatives: putting a curse by a look
decisions.reason: In Scripture an evil eye looks with envy or refuses to give (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15).

decisions.choice: slander: speaking evil of others, and perhaps of God
decisions.reason: The word means abusive speech. In a list of wrongs done to others it most likely means slander, though it is also used for speaking against God (3:28-29).

decisions.choice: sensuality: shameless, unrestrained living; foolishness: moral folly
decisions.reason: The fool in Scripture is the one who lives as though there were no God (Psalm 14:1).

decisions.choice: lying and cheating, shameless living, jealousy, saying evil things about others, living like a fool
alternatives: deceit, sensuality, an evil eye, slander, foolishness
decisions.reason: Readable puts the list into plain words, and explains the evil eye as jealousy.

source.text: πάντα ταῦτα τὰ πονηρὰ ἔσωθεν ἐκπορεύεται καὶ κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον.

records.literal_gloss: All these the evil things from within go out and defile the man.

en.L: All these evil things come out from within and defile the person."
en.B: All these evils come out from inside, and they are what make a person unclean."
en.R: All these evil things come from inside people. They are what make people unclean before God."

decisions.choice: uncleanness is a matter of the heart
alternatives: outward rules no longer matter at all
decisions.reason: The teaching ends where it began (7:15). Jesus moves the question of clean and unclean from food and washing to the heart.

decisions.choice: unclean before God
decisions.reason: As in 7:15, Readable says before whom a person is unclean.

source.text: Ἐκεῖθεν δὲ ἀναστὰς ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὰ ὅρια Τύρου.

records.literal_gloss: From there and having risen he went away into the regions of Tyre.

en.L: And rising up from there, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went away into the region of Tyre.
en.B: Jesus set out from there and went away to the region around Tyre.
en.R: Then Jesus left that place. He went to the area around the city of Tyre, a land where most people were not Jewish.

decisions.choice: having risen: setting out
decisions.reason: The word marks the start of a journey.

decisions.choice: the region of Tyre: Gentile land on the coast, north-west of Galilee
decisions.reason: Tyre was a Phoenician city in the Roman province of Syria. People from there had come to hear Jesus (3:8).

decisions.choice: Tyre, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "and Sidon", as in Matthew 15:21. Some early manuscripts do not, and 7:31 says Jesus went on through Sidon later. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: a land where most people were not Jewish
decisions.reason: Readable tells new readers that Jesus has gone into Gentile land, which matters for what follows.

source.text: καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς οἰκίαν οὐδένα ἤθελεν γνῶναι, καὶ οὐκ ἠδυνήθη λαθεῖν·

records.literal_gloss: And having entered into a house no one he wanted to know, and not he was able to escape notice;

en.L: And entering into a house, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wanted no one to know [it], and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could not escape notice;
en.B: He went into a house and did not want anyone to know, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could not stay hidden.
en.R: He went into a house there. He did not want anyone to know {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was there. But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could not keep it a secret.

decisions.choice: he wanted no one to know: he wanted to stay out of sight
alternatives: he wanted to teach no one
decisions.reason: Mark does not say why. Elsewhere Jesus withdraws to rest or to teach his disciples (6:31; 9:30-31).

decisions.choice: escape notice: stay hidden
decisions.reason: Even in Gentile land his fame had gone ahead of him.

source.text: ἀλλ’ εὐθὺς ἀκούσασα γυνὴ περὶ αὐτοῦ, ἧς εἶχεν τὸ θυγάτριον αὐτῆς πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον, ἐλθοῦσα προσέπεσεν πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ·

records.literal_gloss: But immediately having heard a woman about him, of whom had the little daughter of her a spirit unclean, having come fell at the feet of him;

en.L: But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and she came and fell at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet;
en.B: A woman whose young daughter had an unclean spirit heard about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} at once, and she came and threw herself down at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.
en.R: Right away a woman heard that Jesus was there. Her little girl had an evil spirit in her. The woman came and bowed down at Jesus' feet.

decisions.choice: little daughter: a young girl, said with tenderness
decisions.reason: The word is a small form of daughter, as in 5:23.

decisions.choice: fell at his feet: bowing low to plead
decisions.reason: Jairus did the same (5:22). It shows humility and urgency.

decisions.choice: whose ... her: a repeated pronoun, a Semitic way of speaking
decisions.reason: The Greek says "of whom her daughter". It is one person.

decisions.choice: at once (B); right away (R)
decisions.reason: The usual variation for this word.

source.text: ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἦν Ἑλληνίς, Συροφοινίκισσα τῷ γένει· καὶ ἠρώτα αὐτὸν ἵνα τὸ δαιμόνιον ἐκβάλῃ ἐκ τῆς θυγατρὸς αὐτῆς.

records.literal_gloss: The and woman was Greek, Syrophoenician by birth; and she was asking him that the demon he would cast out of the daughter of her.

en.L: Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth; and she kept asking {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to cast the demon out of her daughter.
en.B: The woman was a Gentile, born in Syrian Phoenicia. She kept begging {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to throw the demon out of her daughter.
en.R: This woman was not Jewish. She was born in Phoenicia, a part of Syria. She kept begging Jesus to force the demon to leave her daughter.

decisions.choice: Greek: a Gentile, a non-Jew who spoke Greek
decisions.reason: Jews often called all Gentiles Greeks. Mark means she was not Jewish.

decisions.choice: Syrophoenician by birth: from Phoenicia in the province of Syria
decisions.reason: The name sets her apart from the Phoenicians of North Africa, around Carthage. Her people had long been neighbors, and sometimes enemies, of Israel.

decisions.choice: kept asking: she went on pleading
decisions.reason: The imperfect shows her persistence.

decisions.choice: a Gentile
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense, so readers do not think she came from Greece.

source.text: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτῇ· Ἄφες πρῶτον χορτασθῆναι τὰ τέκνα, οὐ γάρ καλόν ἐστιν λαβεῖν τὸν ἄρτον τῶν τέκνων καὶ τοῖς κυναρίοις βαλεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: And he was saying to her, Let first be satisfied the children, not for good it is to take the bread of the children and to the little dogs to throw.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to her, "Let the children first be satisfied, for it is not good to take the children's bread and throw [it] to the little dogs."
en.B: He told her, "The children must be fed first and have all they want. Taking the children's bread and throwing it to the little dogs is not right."
en.R: Jesus said to her, "First let the children eat all they want. It is not right to take food away from the children and give it to the pet dogs."

decisions.choice: little dogs: house dogs, pets kept indoors
decisions.reason: The word is a small form of dog and fits dogs under a family table (7:28). Even so, "dogs" was a name some Jews used for Gentiles, and the saying is hard.

decisions.choice: the children first: Israel is to be fed first
decisions.reason: The children stand for Israel. "First" leaves room for the Gentiles afterwards (compare Romans 1:16).

decisions.choice: it is not good: it is not right or fitting
decisions.reason: The word speaks of what is proper, like a household rule.

decisions.choice: pet dogs
decisions.reason: Readable shows that these are dogs living in the house.

source.text: ἡ δὲ ἀπεκρίθη καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, καὶ τὰ κυνάρια ὑποκάτω τῆς τραπέζης ἐσθίουσιν ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν παιδίων.

records.literal_gloss: She but answered and says to him, Lord, even the little dogs under the table eat from the crumbs of the little children.

en.L: But she answered and says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, even the little dogs under the table eat from the children's crumbs."
en.B: She replied, "Lord, even the little dogs under the table get to eat the crumbs the children drop."
en.R: The woman answered, "Lord, even the pet dogs under the table get to eat the crumbs that fall from the children's food."

decisions.choice: Lord: a respectful address to Jesus, and more than that for Mark's readers
decisions.reason: The word can mean sir. She is the only person in Mark who calls Jesus Lord, and she trusts his power over the demon.

decisions.choice: Lord, without "yes", the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts begin her answer "Yes, Lord", as in Matthew 15:27. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: even the little dogs eat the crumbs: she accepts his picture and turns it
decisions.reason: She does not deny that the children come first. She says the dogs are fed at the same time, from what falls.

decisions.choice: says: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark's vivid present. The sense is past.

decisions.choice: get to eat the crumbs the children drop (B); the crumbs that fall from the children's food (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how the dogs come by the crumbs.

source.text: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον ὕπαγε, ἐξελήλυθεν ἐκ τῆς θυγατρός σου τὸ δαιμόνιον.

records.literal_gloss: And he said to her, Because of this word go, has gone out of the daughter of you the demon.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to her, "Because of this word, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter."
en.B: He told her, "Because of what you have said, go on your way. The demon has already gone out of your daughter."
en.R: Jesus said to her, "That is a good answer. Because of it, you can go home now. The demon has already left your daughter."

decisions.choice: word: what she said, her answer
decisions.reason: Her reply is what Jesus rewards. Matthew 15:28 names her faith.

decisions.choice: has gone out: it has already happened
decisions.reason: The perfect tense says the healing is complete, though Jesus is not with the girl.

decisions.choice: healing from a distance
decisions.reason: This is the only healing in Mark done at a distance, for a Gentile child.

decisions.choice: That is a good answer
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that Jesus accepts her reply.

source.text: καὶ ἀπελθοῦσα εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτῆς εὗρεν τὸ παιδίον βεβλημένον ἐπὶ τὴν κλίνην καὶ τὸ δαιμόνιον ἐξεληλυθός.

records.literal_gloss: And having gone away into the house of her she found the child having been laid on the bed and the demon having gone out.

en.L: And going away to her house, she found the child laid on the bed and the demon gone out.
en.B: When she got home, she found her little girl stretched out on the bed, and the demon had gone.
en.R: The woman went home. She found her daughter lying on her bed. The demon had gone out of her.

decisions.choice: laid: lying, perhaps worn out after the demon left
decisions.reason: The verb means thrown or laid. She may have been resting after her struggle, as the boy in 9:26 lay as if dead.

decisions.choice: having gone out: the demon was gone for good
decisions.reason: The perfect tense matches Jesus' words in 7:29.

decisions.choice: stretched out
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps a hint of the strong verb.

source.text: Καὶ πάλιν ἐξελθὼν ἐκ τῶν ὁρίων Τύρου ἦλθεν διὰ Σιδῶνος εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν τῆς Γαλιλαίας ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ὁρίων Δεκαπόλεως.

records.literal_gloss: And again having gone out of the regions of Tyre he came through Sidon to the sea of the Galilee in [the] midst of the regions of Decapolis.

en.L: And again going out from the region of Tyre, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the region of the Decapolis.
en.B: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} left the region of Tyre again and went by way of Sidon to the lake of Galilee, into the Decapolis region.
en.R: Jesus left the area around Tyre. He went north through the city of Sidon. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came back to Lake Galilee, to the area called the Ten Towns, the Decapolis.

decisions.choice: a long, roundabout journey: north to Sidon, then to the east side of the lake
decisions.reason: Sidon lies north of Tyre. The Decapolis lay mostly east and south-east of the lake. Mark does not say why Jesus went this way; it kept him in mainly Gentile country.

decisions.choice: through Sidon, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: the region of Tyre and Sidon, he came to the sea
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "from the region of Tyre and Sidon", which makes a simpler route. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Decapolis: a league of ten Greek cities
decisions.reason: The healed man of 5:20 had told the Decapolis what Jesus did for him.

decisions.choice: north; the area called the Ten Towns
decisions.reason: Readable gives the direction and explains the name, as at 5:20.

source.text: καὶ φέρουσιν αὐτῷ κωφὸν καὶ μογιλάλον, καὶ παρακαλοῦσιν αὐτὸν ἵνα ἐπιθῇ αὐτῷ τὴν χεῖρα.

records.literal_gloss: And they bring to him a deaf [man] and speaking with difficulty, and they beg him that he might lay on him the hand.

en.L: And they bring to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a man who was deaf and spoke with difficulty, and they beg {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to lay [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] hand on him.
en.B: They brought {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a deaf man who could hardly speak, and they pleaded with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to place {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand on him.
en.R: Some people brought a man to Jesus. The man could not hear, and he could hardly talk. They begged Jesus to put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand on the man and heal him.

decisions.choice: speaking with difficulty: hardly able to speak
decisions.reason: The word is rare. It may mean a stammer or near silence. In 7:37 the crowd call such people mute.

decisions.choice: deaf and hardly able to speak: Isaiah 35:5-6
decisions.reason: The same rare word is used in the Greek translation of Isaiah 35:6, where the deaf will hear and the tongue of the mute will sing when God comes to save.

decisions.choice: bring, beg: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark's vivid present. The sense is past.

decisions.choice: and heal him
decisions.reason: Readable says why they asked him to lay on his hand (5:23).

source.text: καὶ ἀπολαβόμενος αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου κατ’ ἰδίαν ἔβαλεν τοὺς δακτύλους αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰ ὦτα αὐτοῦ καὶ πτύσας ἥψατο τῆς γλώσσης αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀναβλέψας εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐστέναξεν, καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Εφφαθα, ὅ ἐστιν Διανοίχθητι·

records.literal_gloss: And having taken him away from the crowd privately he put the fingers of him into the ears of him and having spit he touched the tongue of him, \v 34 and having looked up to the heaven he sighed and says to him, Ephphatha, which is, Be opened.

en.L: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fingers into his ears, and spitting, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} touched his tongue; \v 34 and looking up to heaven, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sighed deeply and says to him, "Ephphatha," which is, "Be opened."
en.B: Jesus led him off from the crowd to be alone with him. He pushed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fingers into the man's ears, spat, and touched his tongue. \v 34 Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} looked up to heaven, groaned, and said to him, "Ephphatha," meaning, "Be opened."
en.R: Jesus took the man away from the crowd, to a place where they could be alone. He put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fingers in the man's ears. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spat and touched the man's tongue. \v 34 Jesus looked up toward heaven and let out a deep sigh. He said to the man, "Ephphatha!" This word means "Be opened!"

decisions.choice: fingers in the ears, spit on the tongue: signs a deaf man could feel and see
decisions.reason: Spittle was widely thought to have healing power. Jesus shows by touch what he is about to do for the ears and the tongue (compare 8:23).

decisions.choice: looking up to heaven: turning to God in prayer
decisions.reason: Jesus looks up before he blesses the bread in 6:41.

decisions.choice: sighed deeply: groaned, with deep feeling
decisions.reason: The groan may be prayer, or grief at the suffering caused by sickness (compare Romans 8:22-23).

decisions.choice: Ephphatha: an Aramaic word, kept and translated by Mark
decisions.reason: As with Talitha koum (5:41), Mark keeps Jesus' own word and translates it for Greek readers.

decisions.choice: says: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark's vivid present. The sense is past.

decisions.choice: Ephphatha, written in English letters
decisions.reason: All levels keep the Aramaic word as Mark does, since he translates it himself.

source.text: καὶ ἠνοίγησαν αὐτοῦ αἱ ἀκοαί, καὶ ἐλύθη ὁ δεσμὸς τῆς γλώσσης αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐλάλει ὀρθῶς·

records.literal_gloss: And were opened of him the hearings, and was loosed the bond of the tongue of him, and he was speaking rightly.

en.L: And his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he began speaking plainly.
en.B: His ears were opened, his tongue was set free from what bound it, and he spoke clearly.
en.R: Then the man's ears were opened, and he could hear. His tongue was set free, and he could talk clearly.

decisions.choice: hearings: the ears, the organs of hearing
decisions.reason: The plural word for hearing is used for the ears.

decisions.choice: the bond of his tongue was loosed: what held his tongue was taken away
alternatives: a bond put on him by an evil power
decisions.reason: The words picture the tongue as tied. Some see a binding by Satan, as in Luke 13:16, but Mark speaks of no demon here.

decisions.choice: were opened, without "immediately", the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "immediately", a word Mark often uses. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: he began speaking: the imperfect, he went on speaking
decisions.reason: He began to speak and kept on.

source.text: καὶ διεστείλατο αὐτοῖς ἵνα μηδενὶ λέγωσιν· ὅσον δὲ αὐτοῖς διεστέλλετο, αὐτοὶ μᾶλλον περισσότερον ἐκήρυσσον.

records.literal_gloss: And he ordered them that no one they should tell; as much as but he them was ordering, they more even more were proclaiming.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} ordered them to tell no one; but the more {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} ordered them, the more abundantly they themselves were proclaiming [it].
en.B: Jesus told them to say nothing to anyone. Yet the more {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave this order, the more eagerly they spread the news.
en.R: Jesus told the people not to tell anyone about this. But the more {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told them not to, the more they told others about it.

decisions.choice: the command to tell no one: Jesus does not want fame as a wonder-worker
decisions.reason: As in 1:44 and 5:43, Jesus orders silence. Here the order is broken, as in 1:45.

decisions.choice: proclaiming: making known in public
decisions.reason: The verb is used for preaching (1:14, 1:45). They spread the news everywhere.

decisions.choice: the more ... the more: the people do the very opposite of the order
decisions.reason: The comparatives are doubled for stress.

decisions.choice: them: the people who brought the man (7:32)
decisions.reason: Those ordered are those who brought the man and saw him healed.

source.text: καὶ ὑπερπερισσῶς ἐξεπλήσσοντο λέγοντες· Καλῶς πάντα πεποίηκεν, καὶ τοὺς κωφοὺς ποιεῖ ἀκούειν καὶ ἀλάλους λαλεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: And beyond measure they were astonished, saying, Well all things he has done, and the deaf he makes to hear and the mute to speak.

en.L: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} makes both the deaf to hear and the mute to speak."
en.B: The people were utterly astounded. "How well {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done everything!" they said. "He gives hearing to the deaf and speech to those who cannot talk!"
en.R: The people were completely amazed. They said, "Everything Jesus does is good! He even makes deaf people able to hear, and people who cannot talk able to speak!"

decisions.choice: the deaf hear and the mute speak: Isaiah 35:5-6
decisions.reason: Isaiah promised that when God comes to save, the ears of the deaf will be opened and the mute will sing. The crowd's words echo that promise.

decisions.choice: he has done all things well: perhaps an echo of Genesis 1:31
decisions.reason: In Genesis God saw all that he had made and it was very good. The words may also be only an exclamation of praise.

decisions.choice: beyond measure: completely, past all bounds
decisions.reason: Mark uses a strong word found only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: the deaf, the mute: people of this kind, not only this man
decisions.reason: The plural speaks in general of what Jesus does.

decisions.choice: How well he has done everything (B); Everything Jesus does is good (R)
alternatives: he has done all things well
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable shape the praise as natural speech.
